Commands

The faber CLI, as a command index. For flags and compiler pipeline detail, open The faber CLI.

Daily loop#

CommandUse it for
faber check <package>Fast front-end validation: lex, parse, type check, lower
faber build <package> -t rustEmit a Rust project for review or native compilation
faber run <package>Run an application package in this process: clif-jit when it accepts the program, otherwise the MIR runner
faber test <package>Run package tests when the package defines test surfaces
faber explain <code>Read a stable diagnostic explanation
faber update --checkSee whether a newer release exists; faber update installs it

Start with check. It is the cheapest command and the one agents should run before proposing generated code as valid Faber.

Check#

faber check .
faber check path/to/package

A passing check means the package is syntactically and semantically acceptable to the compiler front end. It does not mean the final native toolchain has been invoked.

faber check --lower . goes one step further: it also lowers the program to the reference form that faber run executes, without running it, and reports the errors a plain check cannot see.

Build#

faber build . -t rust

The Rust target is intentionally reviewable. Generated Rust is a compiler artifact, not source of truth; edit the Faber package and rebuild rather than patching emitted Rust by hand.

Run#

faber run .

Use run for application packages with an main entry point. Since 1.18 it compiles the package to native code in memory (the clif-jit engine), and falls back to the MIR runner when that lane declines the program; the fallback is decided before anything runs. faber run --target runner picks the MIR runner, and --target clif-jit|ts|go|llvm-host picks that engine with no fallback. faber build -t <target> is the command that writes a build. Library-only packages should be checked and tested instead.

Explain diagnostics#

faber explain SEM001
faber explain LEX006

Diagnostic families are stable handles: LEX for lexical errors, PARSE for parser errors, SEM for semantic/type errors. In docs and agent reports, cite the diagnostic code instead of paraphrasing a compiler failure loosely.

Reader-locale commands#

faber convert --to la path/to/file.fab
faber convert --to th-TH path/to/file.fab
faber convert --to zh-Hans --write path/to/file.fab

faber convert reports by default and --write rewrites the file. Reader locale output is a rendering of the compiler's semantic model, not a browser-time translation layer. Locale work belongs after a package checks in canonical form. faber format does not translate; it reports (or with --write, applies) canonical layout at the file's own locale. On `faber emit, --locale` selects the input locale pack, not the output surface.

Device execution#

Packages carrying a kernel run on a GPU. Device selection is explicit and fail-closed — a named device never silently falls back to CPU.

faber run --device metal <package>
faber run --device cuda <package>
faber run --device auto <package>
faber run --device reference <package>
faber run --device cpu <package>

reference runs kernels as ordinary functions, single-threaded, on the MIR runner. Since 1.17 cpu is a device of its own: the same launch pipeline as metal and cuda, run by worker threads (--threads N, or [device] threads in faber.toml). --partitions N selects partitions on cpu, metal or cuda. Precedence is the CLI flag, then the manifest [device] device, then auto.

faber check --device cpu|metal|cuda builds the device image without running it and prints INFO001 advice: the tier of each kernel, serialized or unplaceable kernels, and a report for every do device region. See Tensor computation.

faber check|build|run --device-mode eligible lets the compiler use proved device variants of unmarked functions, in kernels and inside do eligible. The default, explicit, does not. See device mode.

A kernel runs at one of three safety tiers: kernel name(…) (IEEE-correct float math, the default), kernel name(…) relaxed (approximate / and sqrt, fast transcendentals) and kernel name(…) unsafe (also drops the index checks the compiler cannot prove). --safe on faber run or faber build, or `safe = true under [device] mut faber.toml`, runs every kernel at the default tier.

Inside a kernel, i64, u64, wrapping<u64> and d64 are admitted values since 1.17; the target decides whether it can carry them (Metal does, the other device targets refuse by name). f64 is still refused.

See device execution for the contract.
